sections.title: Status and central finding
sections.lead: The data foundation is accepted for analysis under documented assumptions. All six scored graduate questions now have a computed analytical answer, including Q6's falsifiable definition and Q7's age groups. Scientific uncertainty remains part of those answers: the data do not establish causal effects, unique unmet individuals, or sufficient household access. Sponsor semantics are settled (D-039–D-044) and the organizer prediction file is built and validated by `mi.submission`.
sections.markdown:
The data foundation is accepted for analysis under documented assumptions. All six scored graduate questions now have a computed analytical answer, including Q6's falsifiable definition and Q7's age groups. Scientific uncertainty remains part of those answers: the data do not establish causal effects, unique unmet individuals, or sufficient household access. Sponsor semantics are settled (D-039–D-044) and the organizer prediction file is built and validated by `mi.submission`.

County size explains much of the apparent agreement between estimated need and activity totals. Per-resident activity does not closely track estimated food-insecurity rates. Statewide, reported pounds equal about 106% of the meals Map the Meal Gap estimates are missing (2024), but the median county reaches 64% and the 14 Q6 review counties 42%: the gap is mostly one of distribution, not total volume. Allocation should therefore combine throughput planning with investigation of hidden need and reporting gaps.

The canonical panel covers 86 counties over January 2022–July 2026; Wilkin has no reporting history. Master `Organization.AgencyType` defines the broad network; inactive sites retain historical activity. Six diagnosed keying cells and five negative cells follow D-019, while duplicate reports remain summed in the primary panel. Missing measurements remain missing. County totals exclude unplaceable rows. Current status cannot prove historical closure, and observed July submission dates cannot prove July completeness.

New acquisitions: BLS county unemployment rates, USDA FNS monthly Minnesota SNAP totals, and USDA ERS 2025 SRAM flags. They supplement the cached ACS, RUCC, MMG, CPI, DCYF SNAP and 2019 LILA sources. The optional additional ACS tables could not be fetched because this checkout has no Census API key; the analysis uses the existing county poverty/vehicle/population cache. LAUS contains a missing month across counties; models exclude unavailable controls without imputing them. Source dates, immutable raw files and alternative-source reasoning are in `docs/sources/catalog.md` and source READMEs.

A primary-source timing correction changes Q5: [Minnesota DHS's February 2023 announcement](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MNDHS/bulletins/34b0088) says final emergency payments arrived in March and regular payments resumed in April. April is the main accounting-month event; March remains a sensitivity.

sections.title: Q1 — Do need estimates and activity tell the same story?
sections.lead: **Answer:** counts agree strongly, but county food-insecurity rates and activity per resident tell substantially different stories. On counts, pounds distributed [`PoundsReg`] correlates most closely with Map the Meal Gap in 3 of 3 years and visits [`HouseholdsReg`] least closely in 2; the differences are small and the intervals overlap. On rates no metric tracks need. Broad-network Spearman correlations of food-insecure persons with annual activity (log counts) and county-bootstrap 95% intervals:

Explanations remain hypotheses. `q1_explanatory_models.csv` reports prespecified standardized associations with MMG rate, poverty, no-vehicle share, nonmetro status and reporting-site density (`context`), and the same set plus SNAP participation, mean monthly DCYF persons per ACS resident on the 82 published single-county SNAP units (`context_snap`; joint units are not allocated). These county characteristics explain little: R² stays near 0.10–0.15. The most consistent association is the no-vehicle household share, positive for all three metrics in every year (standardized coefficients 0.12 to 0.22). SNAP participation adds nothing measurable once those are held fixed (coefficients -0.10 to 0.01, every interval spanning zero); tribal caseloads are reported separately by DCYF, so tribal-host counties understate local participation. Poverty is partly embedded in MMG, and site density is endogenous to need and reporting; neither is a causal explanation. `q1_county_concentration.csv` identifies county totals dominated by one site. In those places, visit rules and data entry may explain a mismatch before a county-wide social mechanism does.

**What would change the answer:** core-only, sites balanced over 2022–2024, latest-modification duplicate handling, exclusion of the five largest sites, and complete-measurement county years are computed in the Q1 tables. County rankings are less secure than the statewide rate-versus-count finding. Split labels remain aggregated; MMG offers no matched sub-county benchmark. **Monday:** audit unusually low/high reporting counties and retain need measures independent of throughput.

sections.title: Q4 — Do prices lead activity, and by how much?
sections.lead: **Answer:** there is suggestive evidence for a short response in individuals served [`IndividualsReg`]; a single reliable lag or elasticity across all three signals is not established. Primary Midwest results below are cumulative log-change elasticities over the selected lag window, with conditional HAC 95% intervals. A coefficient of three means a one-percent price change is associated with about a three-percent cumulative activity change in that specification, not a causal prediction.
sections.markdown:
**Answer:** there is suggestive evidence for a short response in individuals served [`IndividualsReg`]; a single reliable lag or elasticity across all three signals is not established. Primary Midwest results below are cumulative log-change elasticities over the selected lag window, with conditional HAC 95% intervals. A coefficient of three means a one-percent price change is associated with about a three-percent cumulative activity change in that specification, not a causal prediction.

| signal | max_lag | cumulative_elasticity | lo95 | hi95 | n | aicc_improvement_over_no_price |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HouseholdsTotal | 1 | 2.099 | -0.712 | 4.910 | 46 | -4.226 |
| PoundsTotal | 0 | -0.490 | -3.026 | 2.046 | 46 | -5.207 |
| IndividualsTotal | 1 | 3.016 | 0.668 | 5.363 | 46 | 0.584 |

Method: monthly log changes; seasonal indicators, workday change, April 2023 event pulse; controlled versions add reporting-site change, SNAP caseload change and a population-weighted county unemployment index. Lag windows zero through six are compared on a common sample using AICc. This shorter prespecified maximum protects a short series from a twelve-lag overfit. Confidence intervals are conditional on the selected model and do not include selection uncertainty. Negative AICc improvement means the no-price baseline was preferred.

ADF checks and lag correlations (including leads as diagnostics) are saved, with Holm adjustment across the exploratory correlations. Differencing reduces shared trends but does not prove stationarity or eliminate confounding. No selected-lag p-value is a confirmatory result.

Calendar cycles persist: workdays and conditional month effects are recorded in `q4_residual_calendar.csv` and the EDA seasonal tables. The monthly coefficients describe differences in growth relative to January, not unique holiday causal effects. **What would change the answer:** price geography, network definition, lag window, missing labor controls and a longer history. **Monday:** monitor inflation with recent activity and calendar capacity; do not issue a precise county surge promise from CPI alone.

sections.title: Q5 — Complement or substitute, and what follows benefit changes?
sections.lead: **Answer:** there is some positive within-unit co-movement between enrollment and visits [`HouseholdsReg`], but it weakens in the core network. Pounds and individuals served do not yield a precise common relationship; benefit-per-person coefficients are inconclusive. The data cannot establish that one program replaces the other at household level.
sections.markdown:
**Answer:** there is some positive within-unit co-movement between enrollment and visits [`HouseholdsReg`], but it weakens in the core network. Pounds and individuals served do not yield a precise common relationship; benefit-per-person coefficients are inconclusive. The data cannot establish that one program replaces the other at household level.

County SNAP and food-shelf users are not linked people. Models include administrative-unit and month fixed effects, reporting-site count and unemployment; uncertainty is clustered by administrative unit. CPI common to every unit is absorbed by month effects and cannot be separately estimated in that model. The caseload includes the publisher's program universe; federal benefit dollars combine SNAP federal and federal MFIP food, with state MFAP/MFIP dollars excluded from that regressor.

Geography: aggregate Dodge/Steele/Waseca activity to MNPrairie and Grant/Pope to Western Prairie. Tribal agencies remain named separate rows, never assigned to host counties. Therefore county-area SNAP exposure is incomplete where tribal agencies serve residents. `q5_tribal_agencies.csv` shows those caseloads separately. The modeled sample drops nonpositive or missing signals and covariates; it does not silently make those values zero. Population denominators use the same cached ACS vintage.

DCYF's documented dashboard lag is about three weeks; FNS is roughly three months and LAUS about one to two months, with revisions. These are approximate source lags, not recovered historical release dates.

### November 2025: what a one-week benefit delay did

During the federal shutdown, Minnesota DCYF told SNAP and MFIP recipients on 21 October 2025 that November benefits would not be issued, then issued full November benefits on 7 November ([Minnesota Reformer](https://minnesotareformer.com/2025/11/06/minnesota-snap-recipients-worry-about-feeding-their-families-as-shutdown-pauses-benefits/); [KTTC/DCYF](https://www.kttc.com/2025/10/16/minnesota-will-stop-processing-snap-benefits-november-1st-if-government-shutdown-continues)). DCYF's accounting-month dollars barely move, so the shock was timing and uncertainty, not a cut. Statewide activity per working day, relative to the previous three months, compared with the same months of earlier years (D-046):

| month | HouseholdsTotal | PoundsTotal | IndividualsTotal | HouseholdsTotal_excess_pp | PoundsTotal_excess_pp | IndividualsTotal_excess_pp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2022-11 | 1.4 | 10.9 | 4.4 | — | — | — |
| 2022-12 | -9.5 | -4.3 | -7.8 | — | — | — |
| 2023-11 | 10.0 | 9.9 | 12.9 | — | — | — |
| 2023-12 | 5.9 | 3.0 | 5.1 | — | — | — |
| 2024-11 | 10.2 | 8.5 | 9.2 | — | — | — |
| 2024-12 | -5.1 | 5.5 | -3.9 | — | — | — |
| 2025-11 | 18.5 | 16.7 | 20.3 | 11.3 | 6.9 | 11.5 |
| 2025-12 | -10.7 | 0.2 | -9.9 | -7.8 | -1.3 | -7.7 |

November 2025 was the largest November rise in the extract, roughly 7–12 points above a normal November across the three metrics, and December fell below its usual level, consistent with part of the demand being pulled forward. The calendar match removes the usual Thanksgiving pattern but not other concurrent shocks; three earlier Novembers are a small reference set.

The exposure event study (same design as April 2023; September/October 2025 reference) finds no larger response where a bigger share of residents use SNAP. The unemployment control is omitted because BLS published no October 2025 LAUS; dropping that month would delete the reference period. A sensitivity without Hennepin and Ramsey (Operation Metro Surge from December 2025) gives the same result. Selected coefficients, log activity per one-SD higher SNAP share:

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| nov2025_delay | PoundsTotal | 0 | -0.008 | -0.065 | 0.048 |

| nov2025_delay | PoundsTotal | 2 | 0.005 | -0.039 | 0.050 |

Interpretation: the delay raised food-shelf demand everywhere at once rather than in proportion to local SNAP use. A statewide month effect is consistent with that, but the data cannot separate SNAP households from others or rule out shutdown-wide anxiety.

**Policy statement:** SNAP and charitable food operate alongside one another; this study does not support treating food shelves as a dollar-for-dollar replacement for benefit cuts. Even a one-week benefit delay coincided with a statewide surge of roughly a tenth above a normal November, which the network had to absorb within the month: payment timing is itself a policy lever. Maintain both enrollment help and food distribution, monitor actual payment timing, and evaluate hardship directly. **What would change the answer:** core-only loss of precision, administrative boundary assumptions, tribal allocation evidence, reporting changes and linked household data.

sections.title: Q6 — A new need-versus-demand measure
sections.lead: **Answer:** a need score built from external county characteristics identifies counties whose activity-rate rankings are consistently below their need rankings. It is an investigation tool with an explicit validation plan, not an estimate of unique unmet residents.
sections.markdown:
**Answer:** a need score built from external county characteristics identifies counties whose activity-rate rankings are consistently below their need rankings. It is an investigation tool with an explicit validation plan, not an estimate of unique unmet residents.

Formula: mean percentile rank of MMG food-insecurity rate, ACS poverty rate and ACS no-vehicle household share. Divergence equals need-score percentile minus each activity-per-resident percentile within the same observed county set. Positive values mean relatively more need than recorded activity; units are percentile points. Equal weights are provisional. No food-shelf, call or market activity is used in the need score itself.

| county | need_percentile | HouseholdsTotal_gap_pp | PoundsTotal_gap_pp | IndividualsTotal_gap_pp | weight_rank_range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chippewa | 98.9 | 60.0 | 89.4 | 61.2 | 1.0 |
| Todd | 77.6 | 66.5 | 59.4 | 58.2 | 15.0 |
| Wadena | 88.5 | 63.5 | 58.8 | 55.3 | 9.0 |
| Swift | 70.1 | 54.1 | 63.5 | 52.9 | 22.0 |
| Lyon | 86.2 | 51.8 | 47.1 | 51.8 | 6.0 |
| Norman | 50.6 | 47.1 | 49.4 | 45.9 | 3.0 |
| Nobles | 92.5 | 77.1 | 78.2 | 42.9 | 9.0 |
| Roseau | 55.2 | 45.9 | 47.1 | 42.4 | 10.0 |
| Benton | 56.3 | 36.5 | 44.7 | 42.4 | 14.0 |
| Aitkin | 77.6 | 33.5 | 53.5 | 55.9 | 23.0 |

Priority flag requires the need score to be above the median and the divergence to exceed twenty-five percentile points in all three signals. This is a declared screening threshold, not a statistically optimized cut point. `q6_priority_context.csv` summarizes rurality, income and population; poverty and vehicle access are constituents and cannot independently validate the index.

| candidate | rank_correlation |
| --- | --- |
| equal | 1.000 |
| mmg_heavy | 0.980 |
| affordability_only | 0.954 |
| access_heavy | 0.981 |

Priority counts across activity-universe and cleaning variants:

| variant | review_priority |
| --- | --- |
| balanced_2022_2024 | 12 |
| broad | 14 |
| core | 13 |
| latest_duplicate | 14 |
| without_top5_sites | 13 |

Counties flagged under every tested activity variant (10): Aitkin, Benton, Chippewa, Lyon, Nobles, Norman, Roseau, Swift, Todd, Wadena. This stability screen uses the same provisional need weights; it is not independent validation. County-level shifts are retained in `q6_divergence_sensitivity.csv`.

Need-score versus activity-rate rank correlations:

| signal | spearman | lo95 | hi95 | n |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HouseholdsTotal | 0.089 | -0.121 | 0.288 | 85 |
| PoundsTotal | 0.120 | -0.086 | 0.323 | 85 |
| IndividualsTotal | 0.139 | -0.076 | 0.338 | 85 |

A rejection test that can be run now: SNAP enrollment requires documented low income and is not an index input, so a need score that did not rise with county SNAP participation (mean monthly DCYF persons per resident, 2022–2024, 82 single-county units) would count against the definition. Rule: reject if the upper 95% bound is at or below zero.

| check | spearman | lo95 | hi95 | n | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| need_score_vs_snap_participation | 0.659 | 0.496 | 0.794 | 82 | consistent |
| poverty_input_alone_vs_snap_participation | 0.621 | 0.454 | 0.761 | 82 | context |
| need_score_vs_snap_participation_given_poverty | 0.282 | 0.022 | 0.502 | 82 | context |

The index tracks verified means-tested enrollment closely while tracking food-shelf activity rates only weakly: it measures something other than food-shelf demand. The glossary counts benefit applications as demand, so this is a check against a second, eligibility-verified channel, not a direct measure of need; the household survey in the addendum remains the decisive test.

The test is not independent of the index: ACS poverty is one of its three inputs and the main driver of SNAP eligibility. Poverty alone reaches ρ 0.62 with SNAP participation, so most of the headline association is poverty. Holding poverty fixed, the index keeps a rank partial correlation of 0.28 [0.02, 0.50]: the food-insecurity and vehicle inputs add SNAP-consistent signal, but only modestly. These two rows are disclosures, not rejection rules.

| year | included_reasons | food_calls | unplaced_calls | spearman | lo95 | hi95 | counties |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2024 | Food Shelf; Meal Program; Affordable Groceries | 3100 | 1084 | 0.169 | -0.027 | 0.357 | 87 |

Calls provide exploratory triangulation only: restricted food-assistance reasons, SNAP Rx excluded, missing county audited. No recorded call is not zero underlying need. Weight alternatives and 2023-versus-2024 MMG ranks show sensitivity. There is no independent representative county survey in the repository.

### Companion measure: meal-gap coverage (D-046)

The rank index says where to look; meal-gap coverage says how far reported supply goes, in one unit. Missing meals = MMG annual food budget shortfall ÷ MMG local cost per meal (Technical Brief: food-insecure persons × weekly shortfall × 52 × 7/12). Meals distributed = reported `PoundsReg` ÷ 1.2, Feeding America's pounds-per-meal standard ([About our claims](https://feedingamerica.org/ways-to-give/faq/about-our-claims)). Coverage = meals distributed ÷ missing meals. The shortfall method changed with 2023 data, so only 2023 and 2024 are compared. Licensed MMG inputs and the exact county ratios stay private; the statewide ratio, group medians and county ranks are published (D-050).

| year | meal_gap_coverage | counties | median_county |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2023 | 1.051 | 85 | 0.633 |
| 2024 | 1.064 | 85 | 0.638 |

| group | counties | median_coverage | q25 | q75 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| all_counties | 85 | 0.638 | 0.482 | 0.924 |
| review_priority | 14 | 0.415 | 0.306 | 0.493 |
| not_priority | 71 | 0.698 | 0.553 | 0.965 |
| nonmetro | 58 | 0.581 | 0.455 | 0.762 |
| metro | 27 | 0.835 | 0.559 | 1.015 |
| spearman_need_vs_coverage | 85 | -0.157 | -0.357 | 0.069 |
| spearman_2024_vs_2023_coverage | 85 | 0.948 | — | — |

Lowest 2024 coverage, by rank (`q6_meal_gap_coverage.csv` lists all counties). Per-county ratios are not published: beside a county's reported pounds they would reproduce the licensed MMG estimate (D-050).

| county | coverage_percentile | coverage_prior_year_percentile | coverage_quintile | need_percentile | review_priority | nonmetro |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Norman | 1 | 2 | 1 | 51 | True | 1 |
| Scott | 2 | 4 | 1 | 1 | False | 0 |
| Swift | 4 | 11 | 1 | 70 | True | 1 |
| Nicollet | 5 | 5 | 1 | 40 | False | 0 |
| Lincoln | 6 | 8 | 1 | 26 | False | 1 |
| Lac qui Parle | 7 | 7 | 1 | 17 | False | 1 |
| Chippewa | 8 | 9 | 1 | 99 | True | 1 |
| Roseau | 9 | 6 | 1 | 55 | True | 1 |
| Nobles | 11 | 1 | 1 | 93 | True | 1 |
| Benton | 12 | 12 | 1 | 56 | True | 0 |

Coverage is stable between years (rank correlation above), lower in nonmetro counties, and lowest among the Q6 review counties, so the two Q6 views agree. Both use MMG and reported pounds, so that is consistency, not independent validation; geography can also drive a low value: Scott's largest food shelf (site 1261) lies in a Scott census block but is booked to Hennepin-Suburbs in the sponsor master (D-047), so Scott's low coverage and its Q1 outlier status are partly a labelling question to settle before any need explanation. Above one is not 'need met': pounds also reach food-secure households (The Food Group's challenge brief, citing the Urban Institute: more than one third of charitable-food users are food secure), residents cross county lines to regional hubs (Steele, Rice, Olmsted, Blue Earth), and MMG assumes seven food-insecure months a year. Below one is an upper bound on the share of the gap filled for that county's residents.

**Graduate addendum:** need is household inability to reliably obtain adequate food, irrespective of whether help is requested. The external-only index is a hypothesis about its county distribution. Reject that ranking if an adequately powered independent survey rules out a predeclared useful hardship difference between high- and low-score counties; reject the hidden-need interpretation if high-divergence areas do not have more food-insecure nonusers with unmet assistance requests. Revise weights/vintages for unstable ranks and audit reporting artifacts before changing allocation. The full prospective design and limitations are in `docs/reference/q6_addendum.md`. The survey tests are proposed, not completed; the SNAP-participation check above has been run and does not reject the index.

**Monday:** begin local reporting and access audits in stable high-divergence counties; review mobile service, transport, hours and enrollment assistance before funding changes. **What would change the answer:** weight and vintage sensitivity, better measurement of access, and the independent survey.

sections.title: Q8 — Does the network fill the retail gap?
sections.lead: **Answer:** food shelves have a measurable footprint in LILA tracts, but presence is far from universal. The unstratified comparison suggests greater targeting of LILA areas; within low-income urban and rural strata, low-access tracts have a lower shelf-presence share than their low-income better-access counterparts. That supports a remaining retail-access gap in location patterns, without establishing household service adequacy.
sections.markdown:
**Answer:** food shelves have a measurable footprint in LILA tracts, but presence is far from universal. The unstratified comparison suggests greater targeting of LILA areas; within low-income urban and rural strata, low-access tracts have a lower shelf-presence share than their low-income better-access counterparts. That supports a remaining retail-access gap in location patterns, without establishing household service adequacy.

| lila_status | tracts | tracts_with_site | footprint_share | lo95 | hi95 |

| 0 | 1284 | 310 | 0.241 | 0.219 | 0.266 |
| 1 | 217 | 75 | 0.346 | 0.286 | 0.411 |

The intervals are descriptive Wilson intervals treating tracts as independent, not valid uncertainty bounds for an administrative census or a spatially correlated sample. Counts and denominator definitions carry more meaning than statistical significance here. Restricting comparison to low-income tracts:

| year | urban | low_income | low_access | tracts | tracts_with_site | footprint_share |

| 2024 | 0 | True | 0 | 90 | 51 | 0.567 |

| 2024 | 1 | True | 0 | 255 | 92 | 0.361 |
| 2024 | 1 | True | 1 | 152 | 44 | 0.289 |

Primary definition: 2019 USDA large-retailer LILA, with one urban mile/ten rural miles and USDA low-income criteria. USDA used 2010 geography and 2014–2018 income data. The Census relationship crosswalk transfers the dominant-area parent's flag to 2020 tracts; `rel_area_share` supports the strong-overlap sensitivity. Historical presence uses only sites reporting in that year, with no current-active filter. ZIP-centroid exclusions, core-only sites and alternate USDA definitions are in `q8_coverage_comparisons.csv`.

Newer retailer-universe sensitivity, using 2025 SRAM flags directly on 2020 geography:

| flag | tracts | tracts_with_site | footprint_share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SD_SRAM_LILATracts_1And10 | 49 | 20 | 0.408 |
| SD_SRAM_LILATracts_halfAnd10 | 211 | 64 | 0.303 |
| SD_SRAM_LILATracts_1And20 | 39 | 16 | 0.410 |
| SD_SRAM_LILATracts_Vehicle | 56 | 20 | 0.357 |
| DD_SRAM_LILATracts_1And10 | 141 | 50 | 0.355 |

SRAM includes a broader SNAP-authorized store universe and provides straight-line and driving-distance flags. It is not a like-for-like trend update to the 2019 large-retailer measure. Its published flags are used; no tract continuous ACS model is fitted. The 2026 network result is a January–July reporting footprint, not an August actual or a certified current-capacity list.

**Monday:** prioritize counties with many LILA tracts without a reporting site, then verify household origins, service areas, hours, mobile stops, transit and capacity. County counts are in `q8_county_footprint_gaps.csv`. No distance is calculated from tract-centroid site points. **What would change the answer:** accurate site locations, client catchments and hours, new retail definitions, or evidence of cross-tract service.
